title: Lists and dictionaries

cells.text: Two Python containers show up everywhere in pandas: **lists** and **dictionaries**. You've already used one without knowing it: `df[["title", "price"]]` has a list inside it.

cells.prompt: Press Run to load the games table. You'll need it later in this lesson.
cells.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("games.csv")
df.head()

cells.text: A **list** holds several items in order, inside square brackets, separated by commas: `["RPG", "Shooter", "Racing"]`. You can store a list in a variable, just like a number.

cells.prompt: Press Run to make a list called genres and print it.

cells.text: To get one item, put its **position** in square brackets after the name. Positions start at **0**, so `genres[0]` is the first item. `len()` tells you how many items a list has.

cells.prompt: Press Run to print the first item, then the length of the list.
Remember, positions start at 0. What will this print? Pick one, then press Run.
Your turn: make a list called colors holding "red", "green" and "blue". Then, on a second line, print the last item (blue) using its position.
hints: The list goes in square brackets. blue is the 3rd item, so its position is 2.

cells.text: A **dictionary** stores pairs. Each pair has a **key** (a name to look up) and a **value**, joined by a colon. Pairs go inside curly brackets `{ }`, separated by commas. To look up a value, put its key in square brackets.

cells.prompt: Press Run to make a dictionary of prices and look up Minecraft.
What will this print? Pick one, then press Run.
Your turn: make a dictionary called prices with Minecraft at 29.99 and Elden Ring at 59.99. Then, on a second line, print the price of Elden Ring. You should see 59.99.
hints: Curly brackets, with "key": value pairs separated by a comma. Then look up the key in square brackets.

cells.text: Back to the table. Because a list of column names is just a list, you can store it in a variable first and then pick with it: `df[cols]`.

cells.prompt: Replace ___ with "price" so cols holds the title and price column names, then press Run.
hints: Column names are text, so use quotes.

cells.text: Dictionaries are how you **rename** columns. Inside `rename(columns={...})`, each key is the old name and each value is the new name. This shows a renamed copy, and df itself doesn't change.

cells.prompt: Press Run to show the first 2 rows with title renamed to game.
Your turn: rename release_year to year, and show the first 3 rows.
hints: Copy the cell above: change the old and new names, and the number in head().

cells.text: You can even build your own table from a dictionary with `pd.DataFrame()`. Each key becomes a column name, and each value is a list of that column's values, in order. For example: `pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Ava", "Ben"], "age": [20, 21]})`.

cells.prompt: Last one: build a table with a column called game holding "Minecraft" and "Fortnite", and a column called hours holding 120 and 45.
hints: Follow the example above: one key per column, and a list of values for each.

recap: A list holds items in order (positions start at 0) and len() counts them. A dictionary holds key: value pairs. Lists pick columns, and dictionaries rename them or build new tables.
